endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Where an AI solution materially influences a clinical recommendation, patients should also be informed of any reasonable non-AI alternatives available to them.

endorsements.title: Ethical and legal implications of implementing risk algorithms for early detection and screening for oesophageal cancer, now and in the future
endorsements.quote: At the point of receiving a letter, an accompanying information leaflet should explain why the patient is being contacted, the implications of testing/declining testing and acknowledge any uncertainties that may arise.

endorsements.title: Reclaiming the Human Connection in Clinical Care With AI
endorsements.quote: patients must be informed, in plain language, that a recording or AI-assisted transcription is occurring, and must affirmatively consent before any encounter is captured.

commentary.bottom_line: Three sources, one framework and two commentaries, endorse telling patients in plain language where AI is used, but no supplied study tests whether mapping AI touchpoints or posting AI-use information through paperwork, consent forms, portals, or signage improves patient understanding or outcomes. No supplied study documents the hazard either, so support for this recommendation currently rests on expert opinion.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The three endorsements come from a governance framework and two commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures patient awareness, comprehension, or trust.

The endorsing sources ask for plain-language notice of AI transcription with affirmative consent, explanatory leaflets for algorithm-triggered outreach, and disclosure of non-AI alternatives when AI shapes a recommendation. These are statements of expert judgment. No supplied study shows whether signage or portal notices reach patients or change their ability to decline AI or ask for a human.

No supplied study tests plain-language AI disclosure in any population, so there is no evidence on whether written notices, consent forms, or signage are understood by patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy. Written materials alone may miss these groups, and that possibility remains untested.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI-use disclosure methods such as consent form language, portal pages, leaflets, and signage against usual practice. Such a study would need to measure patient awareness that AI was used, comprehension of its role, uptake of non-AI alternatives, opt-out rates, and trust. Studies also need to record how much staff time touchpoint mapping and material upkeep require.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems that serve these patients have no evidence on which disclosure formats or languages work. They would need to evaluate their own materials, for example through readability review, translation, and teach-back checks.
